I am a 48-year-old farmer in Quzhou County with middle school education. I have about 8 mu of flat, irrigated land and a small tube well. It is early spring now, and my winter wheat—planted last October—is starting to green up after the cold months. I have been farming this land since I was young, and over the years I have learned that sticking with what works is usually safer than chasing new crops.

This year, I will continue the wheat-maize double crop on all 8 mu. My neighbor tried cotton two years ago and the price dropped; he ended up worse off than me. Wheat gives my family flour for the whole year, and maize always has a buyer at the village collection point. I do not have time to experiment.

For the **winter wheat** already in the ground, I sowed an improved variety—Luyuan 502—using about 30 jin of seed per mu. I did rotary tillage before planting last fall. Now I need to manage it through to harvest in early June. The extension agent told me 15 kg of pure nitrogen per mu is enough, but I usually apply closer to 20 kg because when I cut back two years ago the heads were smaller and I lost yield. I will topdress urea at jointing stage and again if the leaves look yellow. For phosphorus and potassium, I rely on compound fertilizer—I put down about 100 kg per mu of 15-15-15 compound at basal, which gives me roughly 8 kg P₂O₅ and 4 kg K₂O per mu. I will irrigate three times: once now at green-up, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. Water costs money to pump, but three times is what my father did and what my neighbors do. I will spray four times total—herbicide once, fungicide once, and insecticide twice—because if powdery mildew or aphids hit, the whole crop suffers.

After wheat harvest in early June, the window to plant maize is only about a week. I will use **no-tillage** and direct-seed with my machine immediately. There is no time to plow. I will plant Denghai 605, a hybrid maize seed that everyone in the village uses because it yields well and resists lodging. I will apply compound fertilizer at sowing—about 80 kg per mu of a 20-10-5 blend—and that gives me roughly 16 kg N, 5 kg P₂O₅, and 3 kg K₂O per mu. The maize needs two irrigations: one at the V6 stage and one at tasseling. If it rains well I might skip one, but I usually do both to be safe. I will spray pesticide three times—herbicide, insecticide, and one more herbicide if weeds come back.

I expect about 1000 kg per mu from the wheat and 1100 kg per mu from the maize. These are round numbers, close to what I usually get. I thought about planting some vegetables or stevia for higher profit, but those need more labor and I cannot afford to hire help. My son works in the city and sends money home, but I do not want to rely on that for farm inputs. Wheat and maize are my insurance.
